questions.question: Comprehension: Read the following passage and answer the questions given after it. The talks last week between US climate envoy John Kerry and Chinese officials did not yield any agreement. They ended with Chinese President Xi Jinping reasserting that China will reduce carbon emissions at its own pace. Yet, the fact that the two highest GHG emitters have gone back to the negotiating table is a development of note. The talks had been suspended after the Speaker of the US House of Representatives, Nancy Pelosi, visited Taiwan, over which China claims sovereignty, last year. The two sides have indicated that they would continue to hold talks over cutting coal and methane use — a big sticking point in Sino-American climate ties. They have much work to do if global warming has to be contained with the Paris Pact’s target of 1.5 degrees Celsius. China’s climate targets are, by all accounts, consistent with a 3 degrees Celsius uptick in global temperatures above pre-industrial levels. The US’s climate ambition would lead to a temperature increase of around 2 degrees Celsius. US-China differences on climate predate the tensions over Pelosi’s visit. Beijing has traditionally taken the developing country approach that asks rich countries to own up to their historic responsibility for climate change. Things began to take a nasty turn during the Trump years with the then-US President unfairly villainising China for the climate crisis. As part of its trade war on China, the US imposed high tariffs on Chinese clean energy products. The change of guard at the White House hasn’t led to much change. China too has imposed strictures on technology exchanges with the US. A few days before Kerry’s visit, Beijing included gallium and germanium, used in solar cells — as well as in the manufacture of a variety of electronic items — within the purview of its Export Control Law. The strictures on these rare earth minerals, over which China has market dominance, are slated to come into effect next month. While their climate diplomats resumed negotiations, large parts of the US and China have been hit by a record-breaking heat wave. Meteorological reports have indicated the breaching of the 1.5 degrees Celsius target this year — though temporarily. Big power rivalry is holding up meaningful progress in mitigating global warming. In the weeks and months leading to the COP-28 in Dubai, the end of this year, Beijing and Washington must make their climate engagement more meaningful Q37. Happiness, an emotion that is often sought but sometimes elusive, holds an intrinsic value in our lives that goes beyond mere pleasure or contentment. Being happy is not merely a fleeting sensation but a profound state of being that affects our overall wellbeing, productivity, and relationships. Being happy is intricately linked to our physical health. Studies have shown that those who are content and joyful experience a stronger immune system, lower stress levels, and even a longer life. Happiness can stimulate the production of endorphins, the body's natural feel-good chemicals, leading to a sense of vitality and energy. Beyond the physical, the psychological benefits of being happy are equally profound. A positive outlook on life fosters creativity, problem-solving, and cognitive functions. Happiness paves the way for a growth mindset, allowing individuals to overcome challenges with resilience and to pursue their passions and goals with vigor and determination. In relationships, happiness acts as a bonding agent. It enhances empathy, compassion, and understanding, helping people connect on a deeper level. A happy individual tends to spread joy to those around them, creating a more harmonious community. They become not just receivers but also givers of positivity. Furthermore, being happy is not a selfish pursuit. The ripple effects of a joyful life can positively impact society as a whole. Happy individuals are more likely to engage in altruistic behavior, contributing to social causes, and inspiring others to act kindly. However, it's vital to recognize that happiness does not mean the absence of all negative emotions. Life inevitably brings struggles and hardships, and it is natural to feel a wide range of emotions. But embracing happiness as a core value and striving for it, even in challenging times, can lead to a more fulfilled and balanced life. In the end, the pursuit of happiness is not about chasing a perpetual state of bliss but about recognizing and cultivating joy in daily life, appreciating the small victories, connecting meaningfully with others, and growing personally and professionally.
